machines.name: Card punch (Pelerod)
machines.description:
It is used to key data onto punched cards from source documents supplied by the various departments.
It is the first machine used to build the card file that will subsequently be processed.
It consists of:

- A hopper that holds the blank cards.
- A track along which the card travels, fitted with a block of 12 punches for punching the data.
- A parallel track fitted with a 12-brush reading station, used to insert either a card to be reproduced or a card carrying program codes (tabulation, ejection, duplication of constants).
- A stacker that collects the punched cards.
- A numeric keypad for digits.
- An alphanumeric keyboard for letters and digits.

The "punch operator" and "verifier operator" positions were most often held by women.
As a rule they were granted a short break each half-day of work, so they could relax the muscles of their limbs and back.
A good operator worked at a rate of 7,000 to 8,000 keystrokes per hour!
There was a model with memory, called the "PELER MC", fitted with a panel of small relays housed in the left leg of the machine and addressable by means of telephone-exchange-type selectors. The memory capacity was 20 or 30 positions (characters), scanned in groups of ten.

machines.name: Card verifier (Vinod)
machines.description:
It checks whether the holes punched on the Pelerod during data entry are correct with respect to the source documents.
It is built like the Pelerod, except that the punch block is replaced by a reading station fitted with 12 brushes, which reads the holes in the card and compares them with the characters typed on the keyboard, in order to prevent errors in subsequent processing.

machines.name: 80-column interpreter (Trad 80)
machines.description:
It prints "in clear" the holes punched according to the AN7 code: 10 digits from 0 to 9, 24 letters from A to Z (the letters "I" and "O" being identical to the digits "one" and "zero"), and 11 for the point.
It consists of:
- A feed hopper for the cards to be interpreted.
- A reading brush station made up of 80 reading brushes.
- A printing station made up of 80 type wheels.
- A hammer and ink-ribbon assembly for printing the characters.
- A stacker that collects the interpreted cards.
The cards are fed under the reading brushes, 9-edge first.
Printing is done along the top edge of the card, in a single pass, for all 80 characters.
The printing speed is 60 cards per minute.

machines.name: Reproducing and Duplicating Punch (P.R.D.)
machines.description:
This machine is used to:
- Make an identical copy of a file of worn cards.
- Rearrange the data on the card in order to introduce one or more new fields.
- Create a new file by removing certain data no longer needed on the card.
- Punch intermediate calculation results, using a calculator (Gamma 3).
It is made up of 2 parallel tracks:
On the right, a reading track consisting of:
- A feed hopper for cards already punched.
- 3 reading brush stations of 80 brushes each: Selection, Reading, Checking.
- A stacker for the cards that have been read.
On the left, a punching track consisting of:
- A feed hopper for blank cards.
- A selection station of 80 reading brushes.
- A punching station with a "punch block" of 960 punches.
- A checking station of 80 reading brushes.
- A stacker for the punched cards.
A removable plugboard, programmed by means of "plug wires", carries the machine's program for a given application. As many plugboards are needed as there are different jobs to run.
The card is punched all at once, across its 12 rows of 80 columns, by an upward movement of the whole die-and-punch block.
The checking brushes are used to verify that the punched holes match the expected results.
The cards travel through the machine at 120 cards per minute.

machines.name: Card sorter E12
machines.description:
It sorts the cards of a file into a given order (ascending or descending), making as many passes as there are columns in the field to be sorted.
It consists of:
- A feed hopper that holds the cards to be sorted.
- A reading station fitted with a brush holder that is moved to the column to be sorted.
- A horizontal track fitted with a chain that carries the cards along, beneath which is a set of 12 pockets corresponding to the 12 rows of the card. A 13th pocket, called the "reject pocket", receives the cards that have no hole in the column being sorted, or that have not been read correctly.
The column to be sorted is set by moving the reading-brush holder to the position corresponding to that column.
The cards are fed one by one, 9-edge first, under the reading station, which stores the value of the hole read in the column. This value is used to route the cards into the corresponding pockets as they travel along the track.
As many passes of the cards are needed as there are columns to sort.
Sorting begins with the units column, the rightmost of the field to be sorted, then the next one to the left, and so on up to the leftmost column of the field.
The order in which the cards are collected from the pockets is very important and determines the accuracy of the sort.
An alphabetic sort requires two passes of the cards per sorted column (two holes per column for a letter).
The sorting speed is 400 cards per minute.
Other, more recent sorter models have reading brushes instead of the brush holder (D1 to D3, D1000, CS100 to CS103). Their sorting speed ranges from 700 to 1,000 cards per minute.

machines.name: Card collator (Inter B)
machines.description:
This machine is used to build up card files before their final processing on the "tabulator".
It is made up of 2 superimposed tracks:
- Primary track at the bottom.
- Secondary track at the top.
Each track consists of a card feed hopper and two reading stations, each fitted with 80 reading brushes, which, by comparison, allow the program to route the cards into one of the four pockets.
This machine quickly proved to be a key element in the workflow of punched-card data processing. Indeed, beyond its three essential functions, it lightened the file-sorting operations (see the Sorter) required, for instance, before printing a tabulated report.
Merging:

This function made it possible to match two card files, one placed on the "primary track", the other on the "secondary track". Cards bearing the same identifier went to the "merge pocket", while mismatches were routed either to the "primary selection pocket" or to the "secondary selection pocket". Note that the pocket names refer to the names of the tracks.

Separating:

This function made it possible to split one or two card files according to the processing to be carried out. Take the case of two files (one on each track): the cards were then distributed across the four pockets; cards from the file placed on the "primary track" were routed to the pockets called "primary separation" and "primary selection", while those from the "secondary track" ended up in the "merge" and "secondary selection" pockets.

Selecting:

This function made it possible to extract from a file, for example, the identifiers matching well-defined criteria. The file could be placed on the "secondary track" and the set of identifiers to be extracted on the "primary track". Cards from the file were routed to the "merge" pocket when they did not match the selection criteria, while the ones being sought went to the "secondary selection" pocket. The "selector" card deck ended up in the "primary selection" pocket.

In addition to the functions described, this machine could check the sequence of the files fed into the tracks, an essential function on which the smooth running of the job depended.
One can imagine that the machine's possibilities go well beyond the examples given above, making it one of the most complex machines in the punched-card room to program.
A removable plugboard, set up by means of "plug wires", brings the machine's various functions into play to carry out the programmed job. In principle, as many plugboards were needed as there were different applications (payroll, invoicing, inventory management, etc.).
The cards travel through the machine at 250 cards per minute.

machines.name: Tabulatrice BS120 (tabulator)
machines.description:
The tabulator is the main machine of a punched-card data processing room. It combines three input-output units:
- A card reading track.
- A printer.
- An external card punch, linked to it by a shaft.
Calculating facilities enable it to perform the four arithmetic operations and logical operations, and to store information. Programming is done through a removable plugboard specific to each job.
It can also be connected to an electronic calculator to improve its performance, particularly for multiplication and division. The technology is entirely electromechanical.
The tabulator held the world printing-speed record for seventeen years (1943–1960), at 150 lines per minute, while IBM tabulators ran at only 120 lines per minute.
It consists of:
- A feed hopper that holds the cards to be processed.
- A track fitted with two reading stations of 80 brushes each.
- A stacker for the processed cards.
- A selection pocket that receives the cards that caused an error during processing.
- A table carrying 6 to 10 counters (depending on the model), called "totalisers", used for arithmetic (the 4 operations). These counters, each with 12 wheels, can be interconnected in groups of three wheels.
- A 92- or 102-column printer that prints, at 150 lines per minute, documents such as payslips, warehouse stock reports, bank statements, and so on.
A removable plugboard, set up by means of "plug wires", brings the machine's various functions into play to carry out the programmed job. In principle, as many plugboards were needed as there were different jobs (printing stock cards, calculating stock requirements, calculating cost prices, etc.).
The machine has 12 cycles:
- The first, reserved for reading the cards, controls printing and the recording, in the totalisers, of the data needed for the calculations.
- The other 11 (operating) cycles carry out all the additional calculation operations, the extraction and printing of results coming from the totalisers or from the connected calculator, and the punching of the summary card on the "connected punch".
The paper used was generally blank for everyday documents, or pre-printed for more formal documents such as payslips, invoices, orders, etc.
Mechanically coupled to the tabulator is a card-punching machine called the "P.C." (connected punch), which creates the summary cards; these will serve as new master cards in later processing runs, since they carry information updated during the current run.
It consists of:
- A feed hopper for blank cards.
- A punch block, mechanically synchronised with the tabulator.
- A stacker for the punched cards.
The "P.C." cannot operate on its own. As on the "PRD", each card is punched in a single stroke by a block of 960 punches.

machines.name: Hand punch (P80)
machines.description:
It is a small card punch, easy to move from one place to another and to set down on a table or shelf.
It consists of:
- A short track (twice the length of a card) fitted with a rack carrying two stops between which the card to be punched is inserted.
- A die-and-punch assembly corresponding to the 12 rows of the card.
- A "pawl, counter-pawl and ratchet wheel" device that moves the rack carrying the card forward, one column at a time.
- A numeric keypad, above the punch block, with 12 keys to operate the punches and 3 keys to move the card without punching (space, tabulation, ejection).
The card is inserted under the punch block, column 80 first, between the stops of the rack, and the rack-and-card assembly is then moved to the column to be punched.
Pressing a key 0 to 9, 11 or 12 drives the punch straight down, punching the corresponding value in the column of the card currently in position. When the key is released, the punch rises again and, at the end of its travel, moves the card on to the next column. An index shows the column positioned under the punches.
To move the card without punching, the 3 other keys are used:
- E (space): moves the card to the next column.
- T (tabulation): if this device is used, skips several columns and stops at the desired column.
- Red key (ejection): moves the card to the end of the track.
This small punch was widely used in punched-card rooms by the "operators", to remake cards damaged during their passage through the machines, or by the "programmers", to prepare the test decks needed to debug their programs.

machines.name: Card punch P112
machines.description:
This P112 key punch, introduced at the end of 1966, was intended to replace the fixed-keyboard "Pelerod" model.
It had one or two drums into which the "program" card was slipped.
A typical machine of the transition period between electromechanics and electronics. This card punch was fitted with two mobile, removable keyboards, which were nevertheless electromechanical. Being independent of the machine, they made it multi-code, a very useful feature at a time when several card codes still coexisted.
For the verifying function, a similar machine existed: the V126 verifier.
End of production: 1972, replaced by the K212.

machines.name: Card punch K212
machines.description:
The K212 is the ultimate evolution of the punched-card key punch.
It used electronics and optical fibre to provide greater flexibility of use and a quietness of operation unknown to its predecessors.
In 1972, and until 1980, most programs and data were still fed into computers on cards, so production of this machine at the Bull plant in Belfort did not stop until 1977.
This key punch was used, or built under licence, by many computer manufacturers.
Magnetic-tape and diskette encoders would follow, before all this work was shifted onto terminals or PCs, in the hands of the users themselves.
To find out more, see the document by Gérard Lepaul: PerfoVerifGLepaul

machines.name: CR500 (opto-electric card reader)
machines.description:
A card reader with opto-electric sensing.
The last card-based device, the CR500 bridged the transition from the punched card to the transactional computer.
Entirely developed in Belfort, 5,850 machines were built there from 1975 to 1985.
The CR500 is a mid-range opto-electric card reader, economical and reliable.
It has a feed hopper and a receiving stacker, each with a capacity of 1,000 cards.
The brush reading system used in the series 150 equipment was replaced by opto-electric reading devices.
The cards travel at 2.65 m/s past an opto-electric reader. They are read in 100 ms or 20 ms depending on the machine version (300 or 500 cards per minute).

machines.name: Série300 T1 (drum impact printer)
machines.description:
- Speed: 300 lpm (lines per minute)
- Print positions: 120 columns
The first 300-lines-per-minute printer of the print-on-the-fly type (a hammer is fired at the paper at the instant the desired character passes by). The characters move at a uniform speed, with no stopping between the printing of two characters, which brings a considerable increase in performance.
There is no kinematic chain: all movements are driven by synchronised asynchronous motors locked to the master clock of the central processor. As in the series 150 punched-card equipment, the cycle is divided into 15 points.
It has an engraved drum of 120 positions; each drum position carries 60 engraved characters — digits, letters and symbols — corresponding to the 60 possibilities of the 3-hole code (T4). The drum is engraved over 2/3 of its circumference. The passage of the remaining third is used for advancing the paper and re-arming the hammer block.
For each print position there is a removable plate carrying the selection device (a 6-position mechanical memory allowing one character out of six to be chosen for a given machine point) and the striking system; a hammer is fired at the paper, the character being transferred through a ribbon placed between the paper and the drum. Each plate has a mechanical device for aligning the characters on the same horizontal line. The plates are mounted in a hammer block that includes the devices needed for their operation.
Thanks to its two independent (superimposed) paper drives, two forms can be run side by side at different speeds. The movement has two speeds (low and high), controlled by an electronic thyratron device. The final position of the form is indexed by a precise mechanical stop. The paper is driven by "Paragon"-type pin tractors and stored at the rear in a cabinet.
NOTE: initially, this printer was also connected to the Gamma 60

machines.name: Drum impact printer I51
machines.description:
- Print speed: 600 lpm (lines per minute)
- Number of columns: 132 or 160
- Striking: 4-column modules, electrodynamic
- Fanfold paper, punched tractor-feed margins
- Dual paper movement
- Production period: 1965 – 1977
- Quantity: 4,420
The first 600 lpm printer, with 132 or 160 columns, it would be connected to many BULL systems.
It is also the first asynchronous machine: the paper skip can occur at any moment, as soon as all the characters of a line have been printed (on the earlier, "synchronous" models the skip starts in the character-free zone of the drum). In the worst case, its speed equals that of a synchronous machine. It is generally higher; the gain in speed is appreciable because, in a set of 64 characters, the rarer characters are grouped at the end of the drum.
The printing plates were replaced by 4-column modules mounted head-to-tail in the hammer block. All the mechanism found on the earlier models is gone: a column consists of an electromagnet moving a lever that fires the hammer. This principle allows a higher operating frequency and hence increased performance.
The dual paper movement only allows reports to be run side by side; there is a single feed speed. Skips are controlled by a pilot tape.

machines.name: Drum impact printer I41
machines.description:
- 1/4-shuttle printer, working by lateral movement of the paper web
- Print speed: 150 to 200 lpm (lines per minute)
- Print width: 136 columns
- Production period: 1967 – 1977
- Quantity: 4,850
This is a shuttle printer: the drum carries only one wheel out of four. The paper moves continuously to the left, parallel to the drum axis, so that the same wheel can print in four different positions. The characters are arranged in a helix on the wheel to compensate for the lateral movement of the paper during the wheel's rotation. On a full-drum printer, the print cycle corresponds to one rotation of the drum. On shuttle printers, the cycle corresponds to 5 rotations: four for printing a line and one for returning the paper to the right and skipping one line space.
It uses the print module of the I51; the print area covers 136 columns.
The paper is driven by pin wheels, which must also guide it during the lateral movement.
Performance is in the 150 to 200 lpm range; it is a "low-cost" machine.

machines.name: Belt impact printer PR71
machines.description:
- The first printer with a linear character carrier (character belt)
- Belt in an interchangeable cartridge. Belt speed: 6 m/s
- Print speed: 1,200 or 1,600 lines per minute
- Print width: 136 or 160 columns
- The first machine to use integrated circuits in TTL (Transistor-Transistor Logic)
- Production period: 1972 – 1990
- Quantity: 5,000
There are two PR71 models: 1,200 or 1,600 lpm. The print area can be 136 or 160 columns. Its main connections are to the DPS 7 and DPS 8. It was built in 4,833 units and sold primarily on the American market (nearly 2,500 to HIS, of which 1,700 in the USA). It was also sold as OEM to a Japanese manufacturer (TOSHIBA).
It is fitted with a flexible-finger belt (the linear character carrier) running at 6 metres per second. The belt is centred and driven by two crowned pulleys. The characters are engraved on flexible fingers, which reduces or even eliminates the smearing of the printed character on the paper. When the character is struck, it comes to a standstill, the finger's flexibility compensating for the movement of the carrier. Once it has printed, the finger returns to its initial position. Its settling, after oscillation, must take less time than the passage from one column to the next. This is achieved by means of a viscoelastic damper linking the finger to the belt.
The belt is housed in a cartridge (on the disk-pack principle) that the operator can swap, allowing different character sets to be used on the same site. Through coding in the cartridge, the printer recognises the character set in use. Being light and inexpensive, the belt makes it practical for the user to own several, according to need.
The print engine takes over the I51 module. The ballistic hammer is replaced by a pivoting hammer, which reduces the mass involved at the moment of impact and hence the contact time, the flexing of the finger and the smearing.
The ribbon movement is driven by a deformable-parallelogram device to compensate for the lateral force exerted by the belt during printing.
The paper is driven by dedicated tractors to ensure optimum guidance right up to the print line. The maximum speed can reach 1.3 metres per second, obtained for skips greater than 14 line spaces. A motorised cabinet is placed at the rear to stack the paper neatly.
It is the first printer fitted with "custom" circuits, integrated circuits specially developed to handle complex functions of the machine.
Automatic tests and diagnostics, as well as specific tests resident in the machine, are available to maintenance technicians to make troubleshooting easier.

machines.name: Belt impact printer PR46
machines.description:
- Print speed: 400 and 600 lpm
- Print width: 124 or 136 columns
- Character belt identical to that of the PR71
- Spring-mounted hammers, electromagnetic pre-arming
- Production period: 1975 – 1982
- Quantity: 3,600
There are 2 models: 400 and 600 lpm (a few 1,000 lpm machines were built). The print area covers 124 or 136 columns, and it generally connects to the same systems as the PR71.
It takes over the following elements from the PR71:
- The belt and its cartridge, together with the drive mechanism.
- The ribbon movement.
The distinctive feature of the PR46 lies in its hammer block, designed on the principle of an IBM patent. The hammer is mounted on two springs (which allows the flight time to be adjusted by varying the stored energy) and is held in the rest position on an electromagnet (magnetic re-arming). When the character to be printed is about to arrive opposite the column in question, a reverse current releases the hammer so that it strikes the character. When the line being printed is finished, a camshaft re-arms all the columns.

machines.name: Belt impact printer PR54
machines.description:
- Print speed: 800 lpm
- Print width: 136 columns
- Character belt with a guide bead, in a circular cartridge
- Bought-in electrodynamic hammer block
- Production period: 1980 – 1990
- Quantity: 10,000
With a performance of 800 lines per minute over 136 columns, this printer was built in 10,000 units. (That performance also celebrated the 200,000th character carrier manufactured.) The PR54 was connected to all the systems the PR71 was connected to (with a very strong penetration of the US market). Its volume is much smaller than that of the PR71.
Technically, it is a synthesis of the best the printing market had to offer at the time:
- Bull's flexible-finger character carrier.
- The electrodynamic hammer block bought from DATAPRODUT.
The character carrier is modified: a guide bead is added on the solid part of the belt to simplify height guidance on the crowned pulleys. The cartridge is likewise modified to suit this new technology.
A specific ribbon, developed by BULL, replaces the two-spool ribbon. It consists of a fabric band running at an angle across the print line. This band is housed in a cartridge that re-inks the ribbon by means of an ink reservoir.

machines.name: Magnetographic non-impact printer MP6090
machines.description:
- Print speed: 6,000 lpm, 90 ppm, 20 m/s
- Print width: 14″
- Image density: 240 dpi, horizontal and vertical
- Fanfold paper, Carol perforations
